title: Iran Breaks Ceasefire With Surprise Missile Strike on US Forces in Jordan, US Retaliates; Caspian and Red Sea Wars Escalate; Kazakhstan Oil Exports Resume After Drone Shutdown
subhead: Iran's ballistic missile attack on a US base in Jordan ended a 13-day pause in strikes and drew immediate US retaliation, sending Brent back above $90. Meanwhile, Ukraine struck an Iranian cargo ship in the Caspian Sea, Houthis hit Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, and Kazakhstan's CPC terminal reopened after a week-long drone shutdown halved its output.

sections.heading: Iran Breaks Ceasefire With Surprise Missile Attack on Jordan Base
sections.body:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched multiple ballistic missiles at a US military base in Jordan early Wednesday, in what CENTCOM called an 'attempted surprise attack.' Jordanian state media reported that air defenses intercepted and destroyed five incoming missiles. President Trump vowed retaliation: 'We are going to beat the f---ing sh-- out of them.' The US launched fresh strikes inside Iran Wednesday night, its first direct airstrikes since the July 24 bombing campaign pause, according to CENTCOM and multiple news outlets.

The attack killed no US personnel — all missiles were intercepted — but it shattered a 13-day window that had raised hopes for a diplomatic off-ramp. Trump told Fox News that talks appeared to be 'stalling' and warned that if no deal is reached, the US would strike Iran's Pickax Mountain nuclear enrichment site. Analyst Hamidreza Azizi of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs suggested the attack may have been a preemptive signal tied to Netanyahu's White House visit the same day. The Pentagon's casualty database now lists 18 US service members killed and over 642 wounded since the war began on Feb. 28.
sections.whyItMatters: The missile strike and immediate US retaliation confirm the diplomatic pause was tactical, not a step toward de-escalation. With Trump threatening a nuclear site strike and Iran shifting to preemptive missile launches, the war is entering a more volatile phase — and oil markets are pricing that in.

sections.heading: Oil Surges Past $90 as Ceasefire Collapse Ends Price Slide
sections.body:
Brent crude surged back above $90 per barrel after Iran's missile attack ended the brief diplomatic lull, according to Motley Fool and Yahoo Finance. Brent had crashed over 9% on July 28 to a two-week low near $84 on hopes that the pause in US-Iran strikes would lead to de-escalation, Reuters reported. The snap reversal — from $84 to over $90 in under 48 hours — reflects a market that has learned to treat every pause as temporary.

CNBC analysis noted that 61 commercial ships have been attacked in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz, and Gulf of Oman since March 1, killing at least 17 seafarers, according to the International Maritime Organization. At least a dozen tankers were struck in July alone. The IMO data and maritime risk service Marisks both confirm that the Iran-Iran diplomatic 'MOU collapse' has triggered 'the worst phase of this conflict for merchant shipping,' per Marisks CEO Dimitris Maniatis.
sections.whyItMatters: The $6+ swing in two trading days shows the market is pricing in structural disruption rather than temporary shocks. With 61 ships attacked and both sides resuming strikes, insurance and freight costs are embedding a permanent war premium into global oil flows.

sections.heading: Houthis Hit Saudi Tankers and Refinery in Red Sea Escalation
sections.body:
Yemen's Houthi movement fired ballistic missiles at a Saudi oil tanker in the Red Sea, claiming they forced it to turn back, USA Today reported. The NYT reported that Houthis claimed strikes on two Saudi oil tankers — the first attacks since the group declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia confirmed a strike on one of the ships. Separately, Saudi Aramco was forced to shut down its Jazan refinery after a Houthi missile and drone strike, MSN reported.

The Houthis also attacked Saudi oil installations along the Red Sea coast at two ports, while the US held back from launching airstrikes on Iran for the first night in two weeks, the Hindustan Times reported. Al-Monitor reported that roughly a dozen oil tankers were sailing near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and Reuters data showed ship traffic through the strait fell after the Houthi attacks. Saudi Arabia has redirected some oil through its western Red Sea ports to bypass Hormuz — but now that corridor is under fire too.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia now faces attacks on both its export routes — Hormuz to the east and Bab el-Mandeb to the west. The Jazan refinery shutdown and tanker strikes mean the kingdom cannot simply reroute exports around one chokepoint. This double-front pressure on Saudi energy infrastructure is unprecedented in the modern era.

sections.heading: Caspian Escalation: Ukraine Strikes Iranian Vessel, Kazakhstan Halved
sections.body:
Ukraine struck an Iranian cargo vessel in the Caspian Sea, claiming it was transporting drone and missile components to Russia. Iran's Foreign Ministry confirmed the attack killed one sailor and injured another, calling it a 'criminal act' and warning of retaliation, the Times of Israel reported. The NYT described it as 'the first direct military link between the wars in Ukraine and Iran.'

Kazakhstan's oil output was halved — falling from 2.16 million bpd to roughly 1 million bpd — after drone attacks forced the CPC Black Sea terminal at Novorossiysk to suspend operations for a week, OilPrice and Reuters reported. The terminal resumed loading on July 27, with two tankers berthed, though Kazakhstan's Energy Ministry said operations would continue subject to security assessments. CNBC analyst Helima Croft noted that the CPC pipeline carries over 80% of Kazakhstan's crude exports, and the disruption briefly removed over 1 million bpd from global supply.
sections.whyItMatters: Two wars are now colliding on the same energy map. Ukraine's strike on an Iranian ship in the Caspian links the Russia-Ukraine and Iran-US conflicts for the first time militarily. Meanwhile, Kazakhstan's near-total export shutdown shows how vulnerable inland energy producers are when transit states become war zones — and how quickly a single chokepoint closure can wipe over 1 million bpd from global supply.

sections.heading: US Backs Madagascar Rare Earths to Challenge China's Mineral Lock
sections.body:
The US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) committed $4.84 million to Harena Rare Earths' Ampasindava project in northern Madagascar, OilPrice and Reuters reported. The funding covers pilot plant operations, metallurgical testing, and environmental studies, with larger US-backed construction financing possible if milestones are met. Harena estimates total project costs at roughly $150 million.

The Ampasindava deposit is expected to produce 4,000 metric tons of rare earth oxides annually, including 1,700 tons of high-value magnet elements like neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium. A State Department spokesperson told Reuters the US is increasing critical minerals investments in Africa to counter 'opaque, predatory investments from our adversaries' — a clear reference to China, which controls nearly 70% of global rare earth mining and close to 90% of refined magnet processing. This follows a February US grant of $1.87 million to Altona Rare Earths for the Monte Muambe project in Mozambique.
sections.whyItMatters: The Madagascar deal is small in dollar terms but signals that Washington is moving from rhetoric to actual investment in African critical minerals. With China tightening export controls and blacklisting US firms, every Western-backed rare earth project is a hedge against supply chain weaponization — but at 4,000 tpa vs. China's ~240,000 tpa, these projects are years from meaningful supply impact.

sections.heading: Libya's Grid Collapses as Protests Spread to Oil and Gas Infrastructure
sections.body:
Libyans launched a civil disobedience campaign over chronic electricity blackouts, with protesters shutting roads and ministries in Tripoli as temperatures reached 50 degrees Celsius (122°F), MSN and Anadolu Agency reported. Demonstrators blocked roads, shut state institutions, and sealed off government buildings. The protests have since spread to the Mellitah Oil and Gas complex, threatening gas exports to Italy and the country's oil revival, OilPrice reported.

Libya's power grid has been deteriorating for years, but the combination of extreme heat and war-driven fuel supply disruptions has pushed it to breaking point. The country's oil production — already volatile due to factional disputes — now faces the additional threat of domestic unrest shutting down export infrastructure.
sections.whyItMatters: Libya produces roughly 1 million bpd on a good day, and its Mellitah complex feeds gas directly to Italy. If protests spread further into oil and gas facilities, Europe could lose another supply source on top of the disruptions already flowing from Russia, the Caspian, and the Gulf.

sections.heading: OPEC+ Signals Output Pause After September, Pentagon Reclassifies War Casualties
sections.body:
Reuters reported that OPEC+ will likely pause oil output increases for three months from October, after completing the scheduled return of barrels from voluntary cuts. The move comes as the group faces 'potentially difficult talks over new production quotas,' Ecofin Agency reported. Actual OPEC+ production remains well below targets as several members face export and infrastructure constraints — making the pause less a strategic choice than a recognition of reality.

Meanwhile, the Pentagon has quietly reclassified its Iran war casualty database, removing four troop deaths from the official count and adding 142 new wounded soldiers, the New Republic and Task & Purpose reported. The total now exceeds 642 wounded, though critics say the reclassification — splitting casualties across two web pages — makes it harder to track the full toll. Veterans groups warn the move could affect troops' ability to get care long after the conflict ends.
sections.whyItMatters: OPEC+ pausing output hikes while actual production stays below targets means the group is managing optics, not barrels — the real constraint is war damage to export infrastructure, not quota discipline. The Pentagon's casualty reclassification is a transparency issue that could affect both public accountability and veterans' access to benefits.

bottomLine: Iran's surprise missile attack on US forces in Jordan shattered the 13-day diplomatic pause and triggered immediate US retaliation, sending Brent back above $90 and confirming that the war's escalation cycle remains locked in. The conflict's geography keeps expanding: Houthi strikes now close both ends of Saudi Arabia's export routes, Ukraine has directly attacked an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea linking two wars for the first time, and Kazakhstan's CPC terminal is only just recovering from a drone-caused shutdown that halved its output. Libya's civil disobedience campaign has reached oil and gas export infrastructure, and OPEC+ is pausing output hikes not from discipline but from the reality that war damage has already constrained supply. Every major oil corridor is now contested or disrupted — and the diplomatic off-ramps keep closing.
sources: Stripes, USA Today, Motley Fool, CNBC, Reuters, OilPrice, Astana Times, NYT, Al-Monitor, Hindustan Times, Times of Israel, MSN, Anadolu Agency, New Republic, Task & Purpose, Ecofin Agency, CryptoBriefing, Khaama, Houston Chronicle, Iran International, Forbes, Fortune, Convex
